title: 4 Using Secondary Data
text:
So far you have mapped data that you collected. Most of the maps you will meet in geography, however, are made from secondary data: data collected by someone else, for their own purposes, and made available for others to reuse. This week you learn to find such data, put it on a map, and ask whether it is fit for the question you want to answer. This is the skill behind the second GIS worksheet.






ImportantBefore the session



Sign in to ArcGIS Online with UCL SSO (see Open Map Viewer) and have a browser open. Know your fieldwork city: Barcelona if you went on the Catalonia trip, London otherwise. Everyone does the same exercise, with a different data pack.




Secondary data are produced by organisations: statistical agencies, city councils, researchers or companies. Before you use any of them, find out five things. You will need them for your own referencing, and for the critical evaluation the worksheet asks for.







Question
Example




What does it measure?
Disposable household income per person (€)


Who produced it, and why?
Barcelona City Council, to monitor inequality


How was it collected or estimated?
Estimated from tax records and surveys, not a count of every household


When does it refer to?
Income in 2023


Where: for which areas?
1,068 census sections



You usually find these answers in the dataset’s description or metadata page, which is part of why you should always start there and not with the map.



A choropleth map shades areas (polygons) by the value of a numerical variable, such as income, density or deprivation. They are easy to make and easy to get wrong, because each of the following choices changes what the map seems to say:

The variable. Use rates or averages (income per person, % of residents) rather than raw totals (total income): areas with more people will otherwise look “bigger” for no interesting reason.
The classes. The values are split into groups, each with a colour. With equal intervals the classes have the same width; with quantiles they have the same number of areas. The same data can look very different.
The colours. Use a single-hue ramp from light to dark for values that go from low to high. Avoid rainbow palettes.
The scale. The same variable can look different for small areas than for large ones. Averaging over a large area hides differences inside it.




Open a new map (Map) and pick a quiet basemap. Then follow the instructions for your city.



Click Add → Browse layers → My organization, and search for GEOG0187 Barcelona.
Add GEOG0187 Barcelona - Census sections (income). It has one polygon per census section (the smallest statistical area) and these attributes:

disp_income_pc_2023_eur: disposable household income per person, 2023;
mean_taxable_income_2024_eur: mean taxable income per unit of consumption, 2024;
gini_2024_pct: the Gini index of tax income, 2024 (higher means a more unequal distribution).

Add GEOG0187 Barcelona - Neighbourhoods and GEOG0187 Barcelona - Districts: boundaries of the 73 neighbourhoods and 10 districts. You will use these as context.







NoteData source



Barcelona City Council, Open Data BCN (CC BY 4.0), based on the Idescat income account and the INE Household Income Distribution Atlas. Sections, neighbourhoods and districts come from the Administrative units of the city of Barcelona dataset.






Click Add → Browse layers → ArcGIS Online, and search for Lower Level Super Output Area (LSOAs) IMD2025 (WGS84) from gis@communities.gov.uk.
Add the layer. It holds one polygon for every LSOA in England (areas of about 1,500 residents), with the Index of Multiple Deprivation (2025) rank and decile.
To see only London, use Filter: LSOA Name (LSOA21NM) starts with the name of a borough (for example Camden). Add more conditions with or for the other boroughs you want.
For context and for comparing scales, also add Local Authority (Lower Tier) IMD2025 (WGS84) (same publisher): one polygon per local authority, including the London boroughs (filter on LAD24NM). Put it above the LSOAs with no fill and a visible outline.







NoteData source



Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 (Open Government Licence v3.0).







Select the main layer and click Styles.
Under Choose attributes, pick the numerical variable (Barcelona: disp_income_pc_2023_eur; London: IMDRank), then choose Counts and Amounts (Color) and click Style options.
Under Classify data, try Natural breaks, Quantile and Equal interval, with 5 classes each time. Look at how the map changes.
Choose one single-hue colour ramp. Switch off or thin the outlines of the polygons if they clutter the map.
Check the legend: it should say what is being shown and in which units.

Pick the classification you can best defend, and be ready to explain why.




Put the neighbourhoods and districts layers above your income layer and set their fill to none, with a visible outline.
Zoom into one district. How much does income vary between the sections within a neighbourhood, compared with between neighbourhoods?

London users: do the same with the boroughs. Compare the pattern of LSOAs within a borough with the single borough outline. Why might one borough-level summary hide a lot?



Pop-ups should do more than show numbers.

Select the main layer and click Pop-ups.
Set the title to the neighbourhood (Barcelona) or the LSOA name (London).
Show the value with a clear name and unit, e.g. Disposable income per person (2023): €{disp_income_pc_2023_eur}.
Add a short interpretive note: one sentence on what the value means in context.
Click a few areas to check.




Choose one variable from your pack and answer the five questions from Secondary data and where it comes from. Then add two or three limitations. Think about:

Scale: what is hidden by showing averages for areas?
Completeness: are there areas missing? In the Barcelona layer, mean_taxable_income_2024_eur is empty for three sections: why might data be missing?
Method: is it a count, an estimate or a model? (The London index gives ranks: what does a rank not tell you?)
Time: is the year the same as your fieldwork?
Bias: who is more likely to be missing from, or poorly represented in, the underlying data?

Write your answers as notes; you will need them for the worksheet.



Save and open → Save as, with a title like GEOG0187 – Secondary data – Surname. You will build on this map for the second story map.




your main layer shaded by one numerical variable;
a context layer (boundaries) on the map;
a legend that explains the variable and units;
a pop-up with a value and an interpretive note;
notes on the five questions and two or three limitations of your data.




For the worksheet you do not have to use the pack above. Good places to look:

ArcGIS Living Atlas: Add → Browse layers → Living Atlas.
Open Data BCN (opendata-ajuntament.barcelona.cat) for Barcelona.
London Datastore (data.london.gov.uk), ONS (ons.gov.uk) and data.gov.uk for London and the UK.

Check the licence, and always record the name, publisher and year for your references.










Problem
What to try




The Barcelona layers do not appear
Search My organization, not My content, and check you signed in through UCL SSO. Tell staff if the layers are missing.


The London layer is slow or looks wrong
Apply the borough filter first, then zoom in.


The map looks all one colour
Check the classification and the number of classes. Try quantile.


The legend shows odd numbers
Edit the legend labels, or round the values in the style options.


A value is empty in the pop-up
The data may be missing for that area. Say so in your evaluation.

title: 1 Collecting Spatial Data
text:
On the field trip to Catalonia your group will collect its own spatial data: the route you walk, and the sites you record for your Urban Project. After the trip, in the Mapping sessions, you will put these data on a map, combine them with other data, and build a story map. Data you do not collect in Catalonia cannot be collected afterwards, so this week is about making sure everything works before you travel.






ImportantBefore the session: set up and test walk



Work through Before the session below. It takes about 20 minutes, most of it walking. There is nothing to hand in: just bring your phone, with your test walk saved in Strava, to the session.




Almost everything geographers study happens somewhere. Spatial data record not only what something is, but also where it is. A photo of a street vendor is data; the same photo together with the coordinates of where it was taken is spatial data, because it can be placed on a map and related to everything else around it: the route you walked, the neighbourhood it sits in, or census statistics for that area.
Most spatial data take one of three basic shapes:

Points: a single location, such as a site you record or a bus stop.
Lines: a sequence of locations, such as the route you walk.
Polygons: an area with a boundary, such as a neighbourhood or a census district.

Locations are stored as coordinates: latitude, the position north or south of the equator, and longitude, the position east or west of the meridian through Greenwich. Plaça de Catalunya in Barcelona, for instance, is at about 41.387° N, 2.170° E. Your phone works out its coordinates from satellite positioning (GPS). Outdoors this is typically accurate to within 5 to 10 metres, but it gets worse between tall buildings and indoors, which is worth keeping in mind when you record sites in narrow streets.
A geographic information system (GIS) is software for storing, combining, analysing and mapping spatial data. Because every record has a location, a GIS can overlay datasets that were collected separately, such as your sites, your route, a street map and census data, and help answer questions about where things happen and what is near what. In this module we use ArcGIS Online, a GIS that runs in your web browser.



Your group collects two datasets: your route as a line, and your sites as points. You collect each with a different tool:



What
Tool
How it works




Your route
Strava
A phone app that records your GPS track in the background, also without mobile data. You export it afterwards as a .gpx file.


Your sites
UCL Geography Field Survey
A web form that opens in your phone’s browser. Each entry records your location, a photo and a short note, and goes straight into ArcGIS Online, so there is no copying of coordinates by hand.



Everyone records the route on their own phone, so you each end up with your own copy and nothing is lost if one phone runs out of battery. Sites only need to be submitted once per working group, so you will agree who does that.






NoteIf your screen looks different



Apps and websites change their layout regularly. This chapter therefore describes what to tap by its label (e.g. Record) rather than showing screenshots. If a label has moved or been renamed, look for the closest equivalent, and ask in class if you cannot find it.





Do this in the week before the session.



Install Strava from the App Store or Google Play and create a free account. You do not need a paid subscription. Remember your login details: you will need them on the Strava website later.
When asked, allow location access While Using the App.
Make your activities private: tap the You tab, then the settings cog (top right), and go to Privacy Controls → Activities → Only You. You can still export private activities.





Both Strava and your web browser (for the field survey) need access to your location. On an iPhone, both settings are under Settings → Apps:

Strava: Settings → Apps → Strava → Location. Select While Using the App and keep Precise Location switched on.

Safari: Settings → Apps → Safari, then scroll a long way down to Location. Select Allow or Ask, not Deny.


On Android, go to Settings → Apps → Strava → Permissions → Location, choose Allow only while using the app and switch on Use precise location. Do the same for Chrome.




Open the UCL Geography Field Survey on your phone. It opens in your browser; there is nothing to install.
Sign in with your UCL account. If you are asked for Your ArcGIS organization’s URL, type uclondon, tap Continue, then UCL SSO, and sign in as you would for Moodle. You do not need to fill in the survey yet.







TipSave it to your home screen



To find the survey quickly in the field, in Safari use Share → Add to Home Screen; in Chrome use the ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen.






Somewhere outside, open Strava, tap Record, choose Walk as the activity type, and start. You can lock your phone; Strava keeps recording.
Walk for about 10 minutes.
Stop Strava (Stop → Finish), name the activity GEOG0187 test walk, and Save it.
Check that your route looks right on the map, and notice how much battery the walk used.





Your phone, charged, with the test walk saved in Strava.
Your Strava login details.
Anything that did not work, or that you were unsure about.





We start with a live demonstration: your Affiliate Lecturer has done the same test walk with the same instructions, and will show how to get the route out of Strava, how to fill in the field survey, and what the data look like in ArcGIS Online. You then do the same:

Export your test walk. The .gpx file can only be downloaded from the Strava website, not from the app, so use a laptop or computer. Log in at strava.com, open your test walk, open the ⋯ (more actions) menu next to the activity and choose Export GPX. Check that a .gpx file has been downloaded. 
Try the field survey. Open the survey from your home screen and submit one test entry from the room:

Data collection: select Fieldwork - Test.
Group number: 0.
Site ID: S00.
Location: tap Allow when asked, and check the dot on the map is roughly where you are. If it is off, wait a few seconds or drag it to the right spot.
Photo and a short note: anything will do.
Tap Submit and check that you see a confirmation. 

Fix problems. Work through anything that did not work with the people around you and with staff. The troubleshooting table covers the most common issues.
Plan as a working group. Agree who submits the sites (one or two people, so that each site is entered only once) and who takes over if their phone runs out of battery. Agree how your sites relate to your Urban Project theme.
Agree on site IDs. Number your sites S01, S02, S03, and so on, per group, and enter the same ID in the survey and on any notes, photos or recordings you make outside it. That is how you will match them to your points on the map later.

By the end of the session everyone should have exported a .gpx file and submitted one test entry from their own phone.




Everyone starts Strava when your group starts walking, and stops it when you finish. One recording per outing is fine; you can have several.
Submit one survey entry per site, while you are standing at the site, with Data collection set to your fieldwork group (not Fieldwork - Test) and your own working group number.
Charge your phone every night and bring a power bank if you have one. GPS and the camera use a lot of battery.
No signal or no mobile data? Strava keeps recording without data and uploads when you are back online. The survey needs a connection to submit: if you have none, take a photo with your camera, note the site ID and time in your notebook, and submit the entry later, placing the point by dragging the dot to the right location on the map. Check your phone contract for roaming charges before you go.
Be considerate. Avoid photos in which people can be identified, and follow the ethics guidance in your Urban Project worksheet. Do not record your accommodation as a site.




Your sites are already in ArcGIS Online. Before the next session:

Export your own route. Download the .gpx file(s) of your recordings from the Strava website, as in the session. If your recording failed, ask someone in your working group for a copy of theirs.
Share everything else. Put extra photos, videos and notes in a shared OneDrive or Google Drive folder for your working group. Avoid WhatsApp for photos: it compresses them and removes their location information.











Problem
What to try




Strava does not record, or the route is a straight line
Check location access is set to While Using the App with Precise Location on. Do not force-close the app while recording. Turn off Low Power Mode if the route has gaps.


No Export GPX option
Use the Strava website on a laptop, not the app or a phone browser. You can only export your own activities.


The survey asks me to sign in again
Sign in as in the setup: organisation URL uclondon, then UCL SSO. You may need to do this again after a while, also in Catalonia.


The survey cannot find my location
Allow location for your browser (see above), then reload the form. Indoors or between tall buildings it can take a little while; step into the open.


The point is in the wrong place
Drag the dot on the map to the correct location before submitting.


No confirmation after Submit
Check you have a connection, then tap Submit again. Required fields that are missing are highlighted in the form.


Photo will not upload
Try again on wifi, or submit without the photo and note the site ID on the photo instead.

title: 3 Building a Story Map
text:
Last week you made a map of your group’s sites and route. This week you use it as the centre of a story map: a web page, built in ArcGIS StoryMaps, that combines text, photos, video and your interactive map to tell a short story about your theme. This is the format of the first GIS worksheet, so what you build this session is the start of your submission.






ImportantBefore the session



Have the following ready:

your saved web map from last week (find it in Content → My content);
your group’s photos and any videos, downloaded to the laptop you will work on (your group shares these in its own OneDrive folder);
the worksheet brief for this task. The brief is the authority on what your story map must contain; this chapter shows you how to build it.

title: 2 Mapping Your Field Data
text:
In Catalonia your working group recorded sites in the field survey, and you recorded your route in Strava. This week you bring the two together on one map in ArcGIS Online. Everyone makes their own map. Next week you will turn this map into a story map, so make sure you save it at the end of the session.






ImportantBefore the session



Have your route exported as a .gpx file from the Strava website (see After the trip), and know your fieldwork group and working group number. If your own recording failed, ask someone in your working group for a copy of their .gpx file.




In Session 1 you saw that spatial data come as points, lines and polygons. A GIS keeps each dataset as a separate layer, and stacks the layers on top of each other to make a map:

Your sites are a point layer: one point per survey entry.
Your route is a line layer: the track Strava recorded.
The basemap at the bottom is the background (streets, satellite imagery, terrain) that gives your data context.

Each feature in a layer also carries attributes: the information stored about it, such as the site ID, note and photo you entered in the survey. In ArcGIS Online you see a feature’s attributes in its pop-up when you click on it, and you can use them to filter a layer (only show some features) or style it (e.g. colour points by category).
A map on a flat screen is always a projection of the curved Earth, which distorts distances and areas somewhat. ArcGIS Online takes care of this for you; we will not need to worry about it in this module.






NoteIf your screen looks different



ArcGIS Online changes its layout regularly. This chapter describes what to click by its label (e.g. Add). If a label has moved or been renamed, look for the closest equivalent, and ask in class if you cannot find it.






Go to https://uclondon.maps.arcgis.com, click UCL SSO, and sign in as you would for Moodle. Use a laptop or computer, not your phone.
Open Map from the top menu. This opens Map Viewer with an empty map.
The left-hand toolbar holds what is in your map (Layers, Add, Basemap, Save and open). The right-hand toolbar holds settings for the selected layer (Properties, Styles, Filter, Pop-ups). 




Click Basemap and try a few options. A quiet basemap such as Light Gray Canvas or OpenStreetMap makes your own data stand out; Imagery shows what the places look like from above. You can change it again at any time.



All field survey entries, from every group, are in one layer. You add that layer and then filter it to your own working group.

Click Add → Browse layers. Switch from My content to My organization, and search for UCL Geography Field Survey. 
Click Add on the layer, and close the browse panel. The map zooms to the points: you will see the entries of the whole year.
With the layer selected, click Filter on the right-hand toolbar, then Add new:

Data collection is your fieldwork group (e.g. Fieldwork - Catalonia Group 1).
Click Add new again: Working group number is your number.
Click Save. Only your group’s sites should now be visible. 

Zoom to your sites (in Layers, open the ⋯ menu of the layer → Zoom to) and click a point. Its pop-up shows the attributes and photo your group entered.

The filter only changes your map. Nobody else’s data are deleted or changed.




Click Add → Add layer from file, and select your .gpx file.
When asked, choose to create a hosted feature layer (so the route is stored in your own ArcGIS Online content), give it a name such as CAT1_WG05 route, and click Create and add to map. 
The route appears as a line on the map. Check that it matches where you walked. If you have several recordings, add each .gpx file in the same way.




Select a layer in Layers and click Styles on the right-hand toolbar.

Route: keep the Location (single symbol) style, click Style options and change the line colour and width so the route is clearly visible on your basemap.
Sites: change the symbol, size and colour so the points stand out against the route. If you want, you can instead style them by an attribute, but a single clear symbol is fine for now.

Aim for a map that someone who was not there can read at a glance: two clearly different layers and nothing that distracts from them.



Select the sites layer and click Pop-ups.

Set the title to the site ID: click the title, type {, and choose the Site ID field.
Under Fields list, keep the fields that matter (site ID, note) and remove the rest.
Check that Attachments is included, so the photo shows.
Click a few points on the map to check the result. 





Click Save and open → Save as.
Title: GEOG0187 – CAT1_WG05 – Surname (with your own trip, working group number and surname). Add a short summary, e.g. Sites and route from fieldwork in Barcelona.
Click Save. The map is now in Content → My content, and you can open it again next week.

You do not need to share the map with anyone.



By the end of the session your saved map should have:

a basemap of your choice;
your working group’s sites, and only those;
your route as a line;
clear styling for both layers;
pop-ups that show the site ID, note and photo.

title: 5 Describing Data
text:
In Term 1 you used R to describe data and even ran a t-test. The next three sessions go back over that ground more slowly, and with a purpose: to understand what the numbers mean, how sure we can be about them, and when a difference is real. We use one question throughout: who breathes the most polluted air in London? This week you set up a tidy workflow and describe the data. This session and the next feed the first statistics worksheet.






ImportantBefore the session



Have R and RStudio working on your laptop (you installed them in Term 1; Desktop@UCL Anywhere is a fallback). Then run this once in the RStudio console:
install.packages('tidyverse')




Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) comes mostly from road traffic, and long-term exposure is linked to asthma and other respiratory disease. The World Health Organization’s guideline for the annual mean is 10 µg/m³, with interim targets of 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for places still far above it; the UK legal limit is 40 µg/m³. Fine particles (PM2.5) come from traffic, wood burning and many other sources; the WHO guideline is 5 µg/m³.
The values in our data are averages over whole LSOAs: no LSOA as a whole is above the legal limit, but many roadside spots inside them are. Air quality is a physical question, but who is exposed is a social one. Researchers call this environmental justice: are poorer neighbourhoods exposed to more pollution than richer ones? Over three sessions you will describe, estimate and test exactly that.



Your dataset has one row for each of London’s 4,994 LSOAs (Lower Super Output Areas: small areas of about 1,500 residents).







Column
Description




lsoa_code, lsoa_name
LSOA code and name (2021)


borough, inner_outer
London borough, and whether it is in Inner or Outer London


population
Residents (mid-2022)


no2, pm25
Modelled annual mean NO2 and PM2.5, 2022 (µg/m³), averaged over the LSOA


imd_score, imd_decile
Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025: score, and decile within England (1 = most deprived 10%)


income_score
Share of residents who are income-deprived (0 to 1)









NoteData sources



Greater London Authority, London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) 2022, 20 m concentration grids, averaged per LSOA by GEOG0187 staff. Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025. LSOA boundaries: Office for National Statistics. All under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

In the Files pane, click New Folder and create a folder called data.

title: 5 Describing Data
text:
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) comes mostly from road traffic, and long-term exposure is linked to asthma and other respiratory disease. The World Health Organization’s guideline for the annual mean is 10 µg/m³, with interim targets of 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for places still far above it; the UK legal limit is 40 µg/m³. Fine particles (PM2.5) come from traffic, wood burning and many other sources; the WHO guideline is 5 µg/m³.
The values in our data are averages over whole LSOAs: no LSOA as a whole is above the legal limit, but many roadside spots inside them are. Air quality is a physical question, but who is exposed is a social one. Researchers call this environmental justice: are poorer neighbourhoods exposed to more pollution than richer ones? Over three sessions you will describe, estimate and test exactly that.
